newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai debt plans seen raising corporate costs.
newsitem.headline: Thai debt plans seen raising corporate costs.

text.p: Plans to regulate Thailand's short term debt markets may leave many Thai firms with higher costs but should help build confidence in the market, traders and executives said.

The Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) recently passed a ruling prohibiting non-finance sector firms from publicly issuing more than 35 bills of exchange or promissory notes of less than 10 million baht ($2.45 million) in value, if the notes were issued purely for funding purposes, officials said.
The SEC planned to replace this section of the market with credit-rated short term debentures with maturities from 70 days to nine months, officials said.
The proposal, which requires the approval of Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, was to go into effect on November 1.

The moves were part of wider plans to regulate what was until recently an unmonitored market that the Bank of Thailand estimated had grown to provide some firms with up to 40 percent of their funding needs.

No official data is yet available on the market as the central bank has only been collecting data on short term debt issues and transactions since November. But the portion of the market likely to be affected is believed to be substantial, executives said.

"The part of the market with bills of less than 10 million baht is quite liquid. Most of the bigger issues are for commercial purposes, not for funding mobilisation," the SEC's Chief Information Officer Ruanrudee Suwanmongkol told Reuters.
Confidence in the market has waned recently as slowing Thai economic growth prospects, a sluggish property market and high local interest rates have sparked some corporate debt defaults.

One Holding Plc, a subsidiary of Thailand's largest finance firm Finance One Plc in March defaulted on bills of exchange worth $13.5 million, sparking fears of further liquidity problems among Thai corporates, traders said.
They said that while foreign confidence was creeping back into the market this month, most Thai property companies were still unable to tap the market.

"The bills of exchange market has grown extremely rapidly over the last few year, but of late, some offshore investors have reduced their activity in the market," said David Proctor, Chairman of the Foreign Banks Association.
"I think that with the lack of investor appetite from offshore the size of the market has reduced quite significantly this year," he added.

"Recent announcements about how they (the Thai regulators) plan to develop a local commercial paper market will go a long way to replacing the old bills of exchange market, and that is very much a step in the right direction," he said.
But the costs of credit rating new issues and tighter regulation in the market may increase funding costs for already struggling Thai corporations.

"I think this is certainly going to raise funding costs for corporates, the market has been pretty quiet and trade is thin. Foreign confidence was really hit in February and March," said a bill trader at local finance and securities firm TISCO.

Firms unable to issue more bills or to secure a credit rating may have to turn to domestic commercial banks that are currently charging some of the highest rates in Asia. The minimum lending rate in Thailand is currently 13.25 percent.
The SEC said it was confident Thai companies would be able to restructure their financing needs by the November 1 deadline.
"We think six months time is an appropriate length of time for firms to adjust their funding," Ruanrudee said.
